bios.NX-1001: Dr. Mara Voss led the NEXUS architecture team from the program's first month in January 1996. A computer engineer with a doctorate and graduate work in distributed systems, Dr. Voss came to NEXUS from a research program that combined observations from independent technical sources. The interface rules and failure boundaries the regional nodes still follow were set under that leadership. After the July 1998 commissioning Dr. Voss led the technical handoff to OER staff and completed the assignment in January 1999.
bios.NX-1002: Martin Keene joined NEXUS in January 1996 as its systems and infrastructure engineer, coming from research-computing support where the job was keeping mixed hardware and its services running. Colleagues knew Keene for reading the logs before touching anything and for writing down every command. Keene set up OER's first host and recovery procedures and completed the OER assignment in November 1998.
bios.NX-1003: Nate Bell built the network that first tied the regional nodes together. Trained in telecommunications and vendor routing courses, Bell came to NEXUS in January 1996 from regional network implementation work. Bell's reports were short and full of readings: interface names, times, loss figures. The NEXUS assignment ended in October 1998, a few months after the floor opened.
bios.NX-1004: Yvonne Chen was the NEXUS database and archive specialist from January 1996 to December 1998. With a background in information science and a technical research archive, Chen wrote OER's first preservation and recovery practices, including the rule that a backup is not valid until a restore has been tested. Chen kept original values and flagged doubtful rows rather than correcting them quietly.
bios.NX-1005: Elias Trent designed the message and interface layer that moved data between NEXUS's independent platforms. Trent holds a master's degree in computer science and came from distributed-systems research. Trent's notes were dense with sequence numbers and queue states, and grew longer whenever a fault crossed a system boundary. Trent served from January 1996 to November 1998.
bios.NX-1006: Caleb Rusk wrote the early health checks and alert logic that OER's monitoring grew from. An electrical engineer who moved from lab instrumentation into automated testing, Rusk liked turning any repeated check into a script, and liked leaving it running overnight before calling it stable. Rusk was with NEXUS from January 1996 to October 1998.
bios.NX-1007: Simone Laurent brought OER's first outside data feeds into the system. A telecommunications engineer with protocol-analysis training, Laurent was careful to separate what a provider said had been sent from what was actually received, and logged both. Laurent served with NEXUS from January 1996 to December 1998.
bios.NX-1008: Priya Nanduri developed NEXUS's early methods for matching reports from independent sources. Nanduri holds a master's degree in applied mathematics and came from research data engineering. Nanduri's working rule was that an overlap in time supports a match, not a common cause, and the correlation desk still works that way. Nanduri served from January 1996 to December 1998.
bios.NX-1009: Warren Pike set up controlled release and change approval at NEXUS. Pike came from build and release engineering for a research software group and worked from numbered checklists; a release with an unproven rollback path did not go out. Pike served from January 1996 to October 1998.
bios.NX-1010: Helen Sato defined the access controls and audit trails OER inherited from NEXUS. A computer scientist with training in access control and system auditing, Sato was known for careful, unsensational findings that separated what the record showed from what it could not show. Sato served from January 1996 to November 1998.
bios.NX-1011: Victor Hale measured NEXUS's operating limits and recovery behavior through the program's last months. An electrical engineer with graduate coursework in performance analysis, Hale repeated every measurement before accepting a trend and reported baselines with sample sizes attached. Hale stayed through January 1999 to finish the handoff to OER engineering.
bios.OER-1998-001: Daniel Okafor joined OER in January 1998 as one of the first engineers on staff, responsible for the links between OER Central and the eight regional nodes. Okafor came from telecommunications network operations and kept topology diagrams with handwritten changes, circuit numbers noted beside every outage. Okafor served until January 2003.
bios.OER-1998-002: Tom Alvarez maintained the interfaces that let OER's separate sources and services exchange usable data, from January 1998 to December 2001. A computer scientist with an integration and scripting background, Alvarez liked a small working fix and kept dated copies of every script, each with a short note explaining any unusual workaround.
bios.OER-1998-003: Mike Dwyer looked after OER's servers and storage from February 1998 to January 2003. Dwyer came from corporate data-center support and built a reputation for repairs that could be repeated and for labeling every cable. A failed part stayed on the shelf until someone knew why it had failed.
bios.OER-1998-004: Rebecca Shaw was OER's first in-house systems architect and technical lead, from February 1998 to December 2002. Shaw came from enterprise IT operations and coordinated the move from NEXUS development practice to routine operations. Shaw kept an action list beside the terminal and gave every open issue an owner and a due date.
bios.OER-1998-005: Elaine Foster ran configuration and release from February 1998 to January 2002. With a background in technical publishing and software release, Foster kept OER's change history and deployment documents in order, and checked titles, version numbers and file names before closing any task.
bios.OER-1998-006: Linda Carver set up OER's first database and archive handling after NEXUS, from February 1998 to January 1999. A mathematician by training with records-management experience, Carver kept paper reconciliation sheets and followed up every unexplained record count.
bios.OER-1998-007: Judy Price built repeatable data-consistency checks across OER's sources and reports from March 1998 to February 2001. Price came from quality assurance for a data-processing group and never named a pattern until it could be reproduced, keeping before-and-after samples and the exact query used.
bios.OER-1998-008: Peter Sloane wrote and maintained OER's routine checks and automation from March 1998 to February 2003. Sloane came from operations-center support, trusted repeated measurements over a single green light, and kept a notebook of recurring false alarms.
bios.OER-1998-009: Denise Porter established OER's reliability baselines from March 1998 to February 2000. An electrical engineer from a university research computing center, Porter tracked recurring faults in a small spiral notebook and compared current readings with older printouts before calling anything fixed.
bios.OER-1998-010: Marisol Vega owned OER's external data feeds and carrier relationships from April 1998 to March 2002. Vega came from a regional telecommunications provider, kept handwritten carrier contact sheets, and preferred evidence to vendor assurances.
bios.OER-1998-011: Robert Ames was responsible for access control and system integrity from April 1998 to March 2003. Ames came from Unix administration at a financial services company, numbered every paper binder, and annotated each access review with dates and initials.
bios.OER-1998-012: Colleen Brannigan worked communications on the floor from opening day in April 1998 to July 2000. A Worcester native with an English degree, Brannigan came from executive support and a nonprofit hotline, and was known for a composed voice on difficult calls. Off shift: Irish step dance, mystery novels and hiking.
bios.OER-1998-013: Deirdre Maddox stood monitoring on Red Crew's day watch from April 1998 to March 1999. Outside work: half-marathons, cross-stitch and Pennsylvania Dutch cooking.
bios.OER-1998-014: Farah Siddiqui worked monitoring from April 1998 to May 1999. Away from the floor: youth soccer coaching and calligraphy.
bios.OER-1998-015: Gideon Marsh was Red Crew's relief from April 1998 to February 1999, able to take any seat on the floor. Interests: fly fishing, woodcarving and motorcycle trips to the national parks.
bios.OER-1998-016: Harold Pruitt led Blue Crew's day watch from opening day until January 2004. bios.OER-1998-017: Hector Salazar led Red Crew's day watch from April 1998 to July 2002. bios.OER-1998-018: Imani Rhodes worked monitoring on Blue Crew's day watch from April 1998 to June 2006. bios.OER-1998-019: Jerome Atwater worked correlation on Blue Crew's night watch from April 1998 to February 2004. bios.OER-1998-020: Joanne Tillman joined in April 1998 and later led Red Crew's day watch, serving until November 2008. bios.OER-1998-021: Leonard Fitch served sixteen years on the floor, from opening day to May 2014, much of it leading Blue Crew's night watch. bios.OER-1998-023: Paula Ocampo worked communications on Blue Crew's day watch from April to December 1998. bios.OER-1998-027: Terrence Garrity worked correlation on Red Crew's night watch from opening day to July 2012. bios.OER-2001-004: Brenda Ellison was Blue Crew's relief from December 2001 to July 2002. An RIT information technology graduate from a power-plant control room, Ellison was dependable overnight and careful in the log. Ellison was trained by Leonard Fitch. Off shift: baking and cooking for a crowd.
bios.OER-2002-001: Nora Whitcomb joined OER in January 2002 as data quality and correlation engineer and moved to data integration in 2006. bios.OER-2004-003: Phyllis Acosta led Blue Crew's day watch from May 2004 to May 2007. A four-year Air Force communications specialist from Portland, Maine, Acosta was steady under pressure, good at odd faults and kept a clean log. Acosta was trained by Imani Rhodes. Interests: camping and hiking.
